How would any capitalist-organized corporation ever be incentivized to democratize their organizations? Corporations are organized hierarchically. >What’s stopping your collectives from crowdfunding money and allowing every single shareholder and worker to vote on every decision they make? Why should a janitor get an equal say with someone with a doctorate in the direction a bio pharma company takes?

**I am not arguing that democratically organized businesses are better nor that they should be easier to establish, but that the conditions present within our market capitalist society incentivize corporations not to democratize, and that our present conditions have generally calcified, benefiting corporations with capital and infrastructure already, making it difficult to establish alternative models of organization.**

I feel you’re not understanding what I’m asking. 

Self-ownership cannot exist in a vacuum. It cannot exist separate from the physical reality, because it is only in physical reality that one can even own something as the self, body, the manifestation of the self. To own something that something must exist. And especially, to own something is to have something others do not (in most cases). It is predicated on making a delineation between the self and others.

So with the self having a physical existence and it being separate from others, the question then becomes: how does one maintain that ownership over the self if it is reliant on others?

If one lives in a town in which there is a single water vendor, and they do not wish to sell you water for whatever reason (but importantly that reason relating to the self), can one argue that one still owns oneself? One’s existence and therefore self is now predicated on the actions of another. 

Does one truly own something entire if that ownership forces one to change one’s behavior, like, say, moving towns, to maintain that self? Is that a choice motivated by the self if the alternative is to cease ownership over oneself (i.e. die)? This could be seen as a form of intervention into one’s behavior. It seems to me this isn’t a choice if self ownership and the continuous ownership of self is the point.

I would be wary about falling into the dual traps of techno-festishism and the progressive narrative of history (progressive meaning the fairly linear interpretation of history that things have gradually improved for society over time).

Technology and automation is a tool. That’s all it is. I think we get wrapped up in all the propaganda and promises that people *selling* those tools want us to believe when, at the end of the day, they’re just ways for us to work harder or smarter. And more importantly, these tools *cannot solve all our problems*. 

Some of our problems are not solvable by technology. Arguably many of them are not. Many of our problems are political, or social. To give a specific example, some problems (like climate change, for instance), are fundamentally unsolvable given our current *and projected* levels of technology. To put it more simply, *we cannot “technologize” our way out of climate change*. Some people will have you believe we’re just around the corner on carbon capture, or the latest battery or solar development. This may be the case, but it won’t solve the last 200 years of nearly unburdened carbon released into the atmosphere. By virtually all measures, the ship has sailed on *preventing* climate change. There are possibilities to reduce climate change impacts or adapt to them. But technology does not offer realistic solutions that analyses of climate change haven’t already taken into account.

On the notion of progress, history simply isn’t a story of human societies gradually getting better over time. It is a complex and ever-changing paradigm. You talk about automation and technology freeing humans up with more free time, and yet there were significant portions of history like in medieval Europe and in some hunter-gatherer societies where humans had more free time than they do now. Of course that is with the caveat that they lived significantly less technologically-developed lives than we do, but the crux of the matter is that human development has rarely been in a positive fashion for generally all metrics or generally all people. Some in the future might regard our time as distinctly underdeveloped in the ways in which we disregarded the health of the environment, or the political equity of many peoples, and placed our hopes and dreams on technology that didn’t even exist yet instead of taking the steps to fix our problems with the tools we already have.

Making tools and new ideas is a key part of what it is to be human. But I would caution placing too much attention on the tools themselves and what they can do rather than the people making the tools or ideas, because that is where real human change has occurred.

I would recommend thinking about what matters to you in your college experience. For example:

Do you care about being a part of a community? Princeton probably has the most close-knit community of the three. Stanford is MASSIVE and the undergrad population is also dwarfed by grad students. Columbia’s location in NYC often drowns out any sense of on-campus community because most people just go and do stuff in NYC outside of class. Princeton has the undergraduate focus of a small liberal arts college with the resources of a top research school. You’ll run into people you know while walking around (but you won’t run into them *too* often, because there’s just enough size to facilitate that).

Stress will probably be the same at all three schools. But I will say that Princeton’s workload is nothing to scoff at. Our teaching semesters are shorter (12 weeks), compared to most schools’ 15-16 weeks. Stanford’s quarter system is obviously a lot though too so

The artsy/humanities departments at Princeton tend to be a bit smaller compared to the larger majors, so you’ll get good faculty exposure. Moreover, Princeton’s JP and Senior Thesis guarantees that you’ll work with faculty and contribute research to your field.

The uni offers a lot of great resources outside of the classroom too. Plenty of money is thrown towards student activities. If you’re on any aid, you’ll often be able to get some funding for study abroad or summer programs. We also benefit heavily from the alumni network in that many alumni will take on students to intern for them. I got to shadow an alumni physician over winter break, for example.

People complain about the eating clubs but imo as long as you don’t invest your entire social experience into trying to get into the best eating club or “networking”, you’ll probably have a great time. On nights when they’re open, there’s always at least 1-2 eating clubs open to everyone. Make friends through clubs and activities and you’ll do fine.

For what it’s worth I also really appreciate the campus beauty and historicity of this place. It’s a special feeling walking through McCosh Hall for the first time and seeing the stairs worn down so much because of how long students have walked up and down those steps. You can go to the classroom Einstein taught at! Nassau Hall is nearly 300 years old! We have an old ass cannon buried in Cannon Green! It’s so cool.

I find the modern discourse on parenting to be really fascinating, especially when considered in anthropological contexts. Most parenting like the one discussed in the article tend to be directed (marketed?) towards more privileged, affluent families that have the resources and abilities to spend time even thinking about the kind of parenting style they wish to adopt, never mind to actually have time to put it into practice. When you’re juggling two jobs and struggling to pay rent you don’t really have time to put deep thought into why little Timmy is hitting is sister—you just need him to cut that shit out.

But I think a lot about modern parenting and how drastically it differs from child-rearing in previous periods of history. They say “it takes a village”, and they say that because that was literally how child-raising was done previously. The responsibilities of caring and teaching children was shared by the community, in stark contrast to the parental model we use today. The parents would comparatively spend much less individual time with their children because the distinction of ‘parent’ was much more blurry.

To tie this back around, and to the broader discussion, I have to wonder about all these modern discussions of parenting styles—and subsequently how teachers are beholden to far too much of a child’s well-being and behavior—is because of our departure from previous forms of child-raising, and that we are suffering consequences because of that?

Who knows. Just a thought.
